utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning, everybody. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-A, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thanks. Mr. Perisic, can you follow the proceedings, please, in a language you understand? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask for appearances of the parties. First counsel for Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone participating in the proceedings. General Perisic will be represented today by myself, Novak Lukic as the lead counsel; Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith; and our consultant, Mr. Stephane Bourgon; our assistant, Boris Zorko; Tina Drolec; and Marlene Yahya Haage, our intern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. For the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Helen Brady appearing on behalf of the Prosecution and with me today are Barbara Goy, Elena Martin Salgado, Bronagh McKenna, and our Case Manager, Colin Nawrot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady. Mr. Perisic, appeals from the trial judgement rendered in this case on 6th September 2011 by Trial Chamber I, according to the Scheduling Order issued on 24 September 2012, the Appeals Chamber will presently hear the appeal in this case. Before we begin, I note that Mr. Perisic on 29 October 2012, filed a motion on behalf of Momcilo Perisic seeking permission for a legal consultant to appear before the Appeals Chamber during the 30 of October, 2012, appeal oral hearing, requesting that Mr. Stephane Bourgon be allowed to make oral submissions on his behalf during the appeal hearing. After considering the motion and accompanying annexes, the Appeals Chamber grants this motion. I will first briefly summarise the appeal and the manner in which we will proceed today. The case concerns the responsibility of Mr. Perisic for crimes committed by the Army of the Republika Srpska or VRS in Sarajevo and Srebrenica between August 1993 and November 1995, and crimes committed by soldiers serving in the Serbian Army of the Krajina SVK in Zagreb in May 1995. During this period, Mr. Perisic was the chief of the Army of Yugoslavia or VJ General Staff which made him the most senior officer of the VJ. In connection with crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica, the majority, Judge Moloto dissenting, convicted Mr. Perisic of aiding and abetting murder, inhumane acts, injuring and wounding civilians, inflicting serious injuries, wounding, forcible transfer and persecutions on political, racial or religious grounds as crimes against humanity and of murder and attacks on civilians as violation of the laws or customs of war. In connection with crimes committed in Zagreb, the majority, Judge Moloto dissenting, convicted Mr. Perisic as a superior for failure to punish his subordinates for murder and inhumane acts, injuring and wounding civilians, as crimes against humanity and for murder and attacks on civilians as violation of the laws or customs of war. The majority, Judge Moloto dissenting, sentenced Mr. Perisic to a single sentence of 27 years' of imprisonment. Mr. Perisic advances 17 grounds of appeal challenging his conviction and his sentence and requests the Appeals Chamber reverse his convictions in their entirety or in the alternative, order a retrial in relation to specify counts or reduce his sentence. In ground 1, Mr. Perisic challenges the majority's conclusion that his assistance to the VRS amounted to aiding and abetting the crimes committed by members of the VRS. In ground 4, Mr. Perisic challenges the majority's conclusion that the overall strategic objectives of the VRS were criminal. In grounds 2, 3, 5 and 6, Mr. Perisic challenges the majority's findings with respect to the actus reus of his conviction pursuant to aiding and abetting. In ground 7 through 12, he challenges the majority's findings with respect to the mens rea of aiding and abetting liability. In ground 13, Mr. Perisic challenges the majority's finding that he had superior responsibility for the perpetrators of crimes committed in Zagreb. Finally in ground 14 through 17, Mr. Perisic challenges the majority's findings with respect to his sentence. The Prosecution responds that all grounds of Mr. Perisic's appeal should be dismissed. The Prosecution responds that all grounds of Mr. Perisic's appeal should be dismissed. I am drawing the attention of the parties to the questions or matters that the Appeals Chamber invited the parties in the addendum to the Scheduling Order to discuss. Throughout the hearing, counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in any order they consider suitable for their presentation. However, I would urge counsel not to repeat verbatim or to summarise extensively the arguments presented in their briefs. The Appeals Chamber is familiar with these arguments. Furthermore, the parties are obliged to provide precise references to materials supporting their oral arguments. Finally, I reiterate that the appeal process is not a trial de novo and the parties must refrain from repeating their case as presented at trial. Arguments must be limited to alleged errors of law which invalidate the trial judgement or alleged errors of fact which occasion a miscarriage of justice. As set out in the Scheduling Order this hearing will proceed as follows: First, we will hear submissions from counsel for Mr. Perisic for one hour. After a pause of 20 minutes, the Prosecution will respond for one hour. Following another pause of 20 minutes, counsel for Mr. Perisic will have 30 minutes to reply. Finally, Mr. Perisic will have ten minutes for an optional personal address. Parties will present their submissions in the precise, clear, and concise manner. The Judges, of course, may interrupt the parties at any time to ask questions or they may ask questions following each party's submissions or at the end of the hearing. Having now stated the manner in which we will proceed, I would like to invite counsel for Mr. Perisic to present his appeal. Counsel for Mr. Perisic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, General Perisic has been convicted for aiding and abetting crimes committed by the Army of Republika Srpska in Sarajevo and Srebrenica as well as for his omission to punish the perpetrators of the crimes of the shelling of Zagreb. At the beginning I would like to underline the dissenting opinion of the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber who proposed that General Perisic be acquitted on all counts of indictment. This opinion should not be disregarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just wait a second. There is a problem with -- please proceed. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] On the other hand, the majority has made numerous legal and factual errors that we ask the Appeals Chamber to redress with the only right outcome of these proceedings: Acquitting General Perisic on all counts of the indictment. We stand by all our arguments presented in our 17 grounds of appeal, and today we will mainly focus on the issues and questions posed by the Appeals Chamber. However, before that, we want to underline a number of key issues that we believe must be comprehensively and carefully considered in deciding on this appeal. Moreover, Your Honour, one number of these questions go beyond the framework of these appeals proceedings and reflect on some of the key concepts of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, its credibility, and its historic place, its legacy. The first of these issues and one of the most important ones is the overly broad and inadmissible interpretation of aiding and abetting as a form of criminal liability by the majority of the Trial Chamber. The basic elements of liability on the basis of aiding and abetting have been developed through the practice of this Tribunal as a rampart against imposing stands of strict responsibility and support to the fundamental principle of the need to establish individual responsibility. The majority has violated this principle and evidently committed an error, believing that it was not necessary to prove the existence of specific direction in the Perisic case. We assert that for establishing liability, the assistance extended by the aider and abettor must be specifically directed to the commission of crimes. Regarding the requirement that the assistance extended must have substantial contribution to the commission of crimes, this must be proven as the only possible conclusion and not be replaced by generalised findings and assumptions as was done by the majority. The majority committed an error when establishing that actus reus has been proven in this case based on the dependence of the VRS from the VJ assistance for its functioning as an army. This leads to automatic criminalisation of assistance for the purpose of waging war. This is precisely what the majority did, and its findings must be reversed. This is not a case that deals with joint criminal enterprise. The majority has confused liability under the joint criminal enterprise with liability for aiding and abetting. With regard to mens rea in aiding and abetting, unlike the joint criminal enterprise it is necessary to prove that the aider and abettor was aware that his acts assist the commission of crimes quoted in the indictment. Here again, the majority again committed a mistake, an error, failing to consider even the issue whether Mr. Perisic knew that the assistance extended by the VJ aided the commission of crimes by the VRS in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. A very important issue is reconsidering the effective control, effective control inquiry by the majority. The appellant claims in accordance with the dissenting opinion of Judge Moloto that personal and mutual admission of the existence of the relationship subordinate-superior must be proven. That is a test of effective control. The relationship between superior and subordinate cannot exist if the superior and the subordinate do not share the conviction and do not act as if they are in such a relationship. And finally, Your Honours, if the Appeals Chamber finally establishes the responsibility of General Perisic regarding the crimes for which he was accused, then of key importance is that the Chamber should reconsider the multiple errors committed by the majority in concluding on the obviously unreasonable sentence. Now I will give the floor to Mr. Guy-Smith, who will present our responses to your questions numbers 1 through 4, after which Mr. Bourgon will take the floor, taking issue number 5, and then I will present additional arguments considering the errors committed by the majority on sentencing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Guy-Smith, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I first of all note that we have apparently new equipment for purposes of listening and talking to each other, and it says vote now, and I suggest to you at the very beginning you can vote now for the Defence. You've asked a number of questions and what I'm going to do is I'm going to respond directly to the questions that you've asked in the order that they have been asked, the first being how the Appeals Chamber should address the issue of specific direction in the context of aiding and abetting liability. The Trial Chamber majority engaged in demonstrable legal error in removing the requirement of specific direction in its determination of General Perisic's liability under an aiding and abetting analysis. The prejudice is clear. Had the correct standard been applied he would have been acquitted because there was no proof of specific direction. Specific direction is an integral, important component in the analysis of aiding and abetting. Its excision is a dangerous and radical departure that threatens the basic concept of individual responsibility. The precedent in its absence establishes -- is unsettling and far reaching. You should refine the language of previous decisions to clarify the long-standing and oft repeated principle of law that the actus reus for aiding and abetting requires proving two prongs: First, specific direction to assist and, second, substantial effect on the commission of crimes. I digress for a very brief moment, because throughout the opinions that have been written in -- in this Tribunal and throughout the opinions that have been written at the ICTR, in each and every one of the opinions that I'll be mentioning the language is specific direction and substantial effect. That's conjunctive pleading, as I would say. It isn't "or," it's "and." So both of these components must be met and it's throughout your decision on law. The jurisprudence articulating the specific direction which you sometimes framed as specific assistance directed or specifically aimed is one of two prongs necessary in determining whether aiding and abetting has been proved beyond a reasonable out with regard to the actus reus elements has remained relatively consistent since Tadic; Delalic, paragraph 344; Kupreskic, paragraph 248; Blaskic, 45; Simic, 85; Blagojevic, 222; Oric, paragraph 43. There is, of course, an exception. That's -- the exception with the majority in our case relied on and that's Mrksic. But Mrksic rose in a completely different context concerning the issue of actus reus. In Mrksic it was raised regarding the mens rea for aiding and abetting by omission, which is not our case. It has nothing to do with our case. But even the Mrksic Chamber acknowledged the important of the requirement of the direction stating that: "The fact that an omission must be," and I emphasise "directed to assist, encourage, or lend moral support to the perpetration of a crime forms part of the actus reus, not the mens rea of aiding and abetting, but the language of directed once again is there." That's paragraph 159, quoting Oric, paragraph 43. So even the Mrksic Chamber included requirement of direction. Therefore, based on that law, the fact that the aid was specifically directed towards a crime committed must be proved beyond reasonable doubt whether or not it is considered stricto senso to be an essential element. We do, of course, maintain that it is. However, even if specific direction was not considered to be an essential element in and of itself, it is implied in the analysis. Therefore, specific direction still must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt before any finding that an individual aided and abetted a crime or crimes can occur. The Trial Chamber's majority reliance on Mrksic in paragraph 126 we maintain is a departure from the applicable law. It is incorrect. It constitutes legal error. The jurisprudence of the ICTR also continues to supply a specificity standard in its analysis for determining whether the actus reus of aiding and abetting has been proven or not, and I apologise to those who speak the language better than I do for my mispronunciation of some of these cases. See Ntawukulilyayo, paragraph 214, a case that was decided after Mrksic. Kalimanzira, a case decided after Mrksic. Rukundo a case decided after Mrksic. The paragraphs for the previous are 74 for Kalimanzira, 54 for Rukundo. Also see Seromba at paragraph 44. Nahimana, at paragraph 214. I'm sorry. Nahimana, paragraph 42, Ntagerura which I believe is paragraph 74. I will have to double-check that. And Ntakirutimana, which is at paragraphs 530 and 532. In each and every one of those cases you have used the language specifically directed or one of the other forms of that that I have mentioned previously and substantial effect. So specific direction remains again and again and again. The wordings of Article 6.1 of the ICTR statute and 7.1 of our statute are identical. And I think if you review the cases just mentioned you'll see the composition of the appeals bench is similarly so. So there is really no logical reason why the Appeals Chamber would continue to include specific direction or aim in the definition of the actus reus in aiding and abetting after Mrksic if in fact it's not a requirement. Obviously it is. A proper construction of the statute taking due account of its purpose requires the conclusion that in the interests of certainty and predictability the Appeals Chamber should follow its previous decisions taken on the jurisprudential path articulated since Tadic clarifying in the instant case and henceforth that specific direction must be proven. And I take solace in the teachings of this Chamber from Aleksovski. I paraphrase paragraph 107. There are a number of consequences here departing from this well recognised test in failing to articulate that specific direction is an integral and indeed a component part of aiding and abetting liability. First, there is no direct link between the assistance given and the crime committed. There's a question that exists in all trials. What is a specific direction in practical terms? And what must the trier of fact look for to determine whether it has or has not been proved? In this regard, we refer you to the dissenting opinion of Judge Moloto who has defined specific direction as the existence of a direct link between a practical assistance provided, the aid and the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I just realised that. I do apologise. That's at paragraph 10. Absent such a direct link it cannot be said that the aid was specifically directed towards the commission of the crime. The existence of a direct link between the aid given and the crime committed is not the same as proof of a cause-effect relationship between the conduct of the aider abettor and the commission of the crime. That's the condition sine qua non which is a more stringent requirement which has been rejected in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. Specific direction however is something different. It requires a direct link between the practical assistance provided and the crime committed. In the sense of the practical assistance provided in and of itself directly assisted the crime. Second, under the majority's holding, a finding of guilt can be imposed whether the assistance given is temporally or geographically remote to the crime committed irrespective of any intervening causes. In cases where practical assistance was provided to the principal perpetrator from a remote location or a much earlier time, it is all the more important to prove that the practical assistance was specifically directed to the commission of the crime. In this we fully agree with Judge Moloto's dissenting opinion in paragraph 10. But furthermore the Kupreskic case is instructive in this regard. There you found that Kupreskic acts of unloading weapons from his car was not sufficient for finding that his acts were acts specifically directed towards the -- assisting the crime of persecution. You took into account the passage of time between the act and the criminal activity, explaining the six month length of time between when Kupreskic was observed unloading the weapons and when the attack on Ahmici actually occurred diminishes the likelihood that the weapons were intended to be used for attacking the Muslim population. Paragraph 277. Similarly, Kalimanzira's conviction for aiding and abetting genocide was quashed because of the lack of any proven immediate connection between his speech and specific killings. That's at paragraph 923. We contend that these cases establish that specific direction must be considered an explicit component because otherwise there's a missing link between the accused's acts and the crime. And third, if the actus reus of aiding and abetting is reduced solely to a consideration of substantial effect on the commission of the crime, a mere knowledge standard is wholly inadequate to impose individual assessorial liability. Whether or not you accept our argument in ground 7 that purpose is and has been customary international law standard for the mens rea prong of the test, without inclusion of specific direction as part of the actus reus analysis in the law of aiding and abetting in real terms what occurs is that this law runs dangerously close to diluting the minimal standards necessary for the requirement of individual culpability. Without specific direction, mere knowledge of a crime and any assistance which had a substantial effect on the commission of a crime would result in a conviction even if that assistance was not meant to assist any crime. Such a standard fails to establish a minimal threshold of behaviour for liability. Part is rendering assistance will not know what behaviour is legally appropriate and what is legally prohibited. Objectively speaking, the practical effect can be demonstrated by some examples from the events of the past 12 months. The arming and training of the Sudanese in the DRC military police and security personnel while embargoes were in place, or give rise to aiding and abetting liability for British officials. I need not remind you of the situation in Darfur and the indictment against Omar Bashir. United Kingdom officials have known of the knowledge of crimes have been committed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And have been rendering assistance for the past five years there. In rending vital and critical assistance to the Libyan rebels to overthrow the previous regime with knowledge of by crimes being committed by the selfsame rebel forces, leaders in France, the United States, United Kingdom, and NATO, to name but a few, would be liable for aiding and abetting any or all of their crimes. Inasmuch as British Secretary Hague may wish to cast the assistance as humanitarian given to the forces in Syria the training and communication assistance given to the opposition forces with full knowledge of those crimes being commit by rebel forces there subjects those giving assistance to aiding and abetting liability. In effect, if the majority's holding is upheld in this case, the result is clear. Any and all officials, political or military, with mere knowledge that crimes were being committed who facilitate assistance to foreign armies, state or non-state, during a conflict will be liable for aiding and abetting any crimes committed by those they assist. We do not believe the jurisprudence of this institution would lend any support even if inadvertent to such an absurd state of affairs. Specifically direction insulates against this. It makes clear that the assistance must be directly linked to committing the crime consistent with the requirement of individual liability. The majority's finding in this case is specific direction was not required was clearly erroneous and clearly prejudicial. Turning to your second question: Whether aid that is not specifically directed toward a particular crime can have a substantial effect required to enter a conviction for aiding and abetting. Following the discussion regarding specific direction the answer to this question is very simply no. In the absence of specific direction substantial effect alone, no matter how substantial the effect of practical assistance turns out to be, is insufficient to enter a conviction for aiding and abetting. To find otherwise effectively eviscerates the requirement of individual criminal responsibility and this case highlights why. To paraphrase --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: May I ask you a question on this prong of substantial effect. Given the massive nature of the aid provided by the VRS, what kind of aid would you yourself consider sufficiently substantial to meet the threshold required for conviction for aiding and abetting?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if I can answer that question in the abstract and I'll tell you why, Your Honour. The difficulty with that is that during a time of conflict, the amount of -- of supplies or logistic assistance that was given or is given in any conflict situation I don't believe is necessarily quantified, and I haven't been able to find anyone who can tell me how it would be quantified with regard to the issue of used for legitimate military purposes. So when you ask the question of how much would be sufficient in the context of a -- in the context of a war that's being waged it's virtually impossible to put a figure on that. I will be attending to the issue of substantial effect because I believe that's directly related to the fourth question you've asked and I think I may be able to pick up some more of it there. I'm appreciative of your question though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: What I'm curious about is if you look at sort of a spectrum of various kinds of aid, is there a point somewhere on that spectrum where the magnitude of the aid reaches such proportions that it's sort of obvious that aid must by its very nature have substantial effect on the commission of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think you can make that analysis and I -- once again I understand what your question is. I think in some senses you're really asking, kind of, what I would call the question of how long does a fire maintain itself, and is there a point in time when a fire will burn itself out, and the answer to that question is obviously as long as there's fuel for the fire, the fire will continue to burn, but in the history of human behaviour, in our entire history we have never seemed to be in a situation where it's the lack of some kind of assistance that has the fire burn out. It seems to occur for entirely different reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. One cannot simply ignore the reality that relations between states are often reinforced by the provision of significant military aid. Many foreign armies are dependent to various degrees upon such assistance to function. In this context, in many conflict zones around the world, the provision of military aim, aid is aimed at supporting mutual interests such as the terms of war, the promotion of regional and global peace, stability, prosperity, and other objectives. That's paragraph 32 of Judge Moloto's dissent. If effect if the effect of the aid given becomes a sole litmus test for conviction pursuant to the law of aiding and abetting which I think goes somewhat to the question you've asked, Your Honour, then all military and political leaders who support the provision of logistical assistance to a foreign army dependent on such assistance irrespective of a quantitative amount will be liable for aiding and abetting should any war crimes or crimes against humanity occur. Unfortunately, as they inevitably do in all wars, unfortunately. Turning to your third question whether the aid facilitated by Mr. Perisic met the requirements of specific direction, if any, in the context of aiding and abetting liability. The aid facilitated by Perisic did not meet the requirements of specific direction, if any, and the majority erred in so finding. No evidence was presented that any of the assistance given was specifically directed at providing practical assistance to the perpetration of crimes in Sarajevo or Srebrenica, and your reasoning in Kupreskic which was discussed in relation to question number 1 demonstrates that not any act of assistance constitutes aiding and abetting. Only acts that are specifically directed towards assisting a crime is sufficient. The evidence establishes that the assistance given was in the context of supporting the war effort and the judgement is replete with paragraphs referring to that, such as paragraphs 107, 109, 1234, that he oversaw a -- assist in providing comprehensive military assistance, 1235, 1236, 1237, 1365 attempt to accept -- attempt to have people accept peace, 1366, 1369, attempt to persuade Mladic to accept peace which is important in the context of a war, because these are the activities that are being engaged in. 1406, 1407, 1408, 1411 and -12 when there are meetings with prominent members of the RSK and RS. Again for the purpose we would contend, if not at least for peace. 1414, 1597, 1598. 1599 which I think goes to some of what you were referring to again, Your Honour, in terms of specific -- and I'm analysing this under the rubric of specific direction -- could not have waged war if the assistance had been withheld, could not have survived or defended its territory. That's what it was directed towards. That's why the assistance existed. And that's what the majority found repeatedly throughout this judgement. 1602, the VJ depended heavily on FRY and VJ assistance -- the VRS depended heavily on FRY and VJ assistance in order to function as an army and wage war. All of this established that the aid facilitated to support the war effort not the specific direction for a crime. With the above in mind examination of the aid facilitated by Perisic fails to meet the specific direction prong of the test for finding aiding and abetting liability. Looking at first of all personnel. The evidence was that all but three of the VJ corps members were sent to the VRS before General Perisic became Chief of Staff. There was no proof that those three members were involved in the commission of crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. It certainly cannot be said that personnel based on that was the -- that the use of the provision of personnel based on those facts was proof beyond a reasonable doubt that the assistance provided by Perisic was specifically directed to the commission of crimes in these locations. Financial assistance and benefits, there was no link proved between this sort of practical assistance. That the payment of the salaries were great help to the VRS, at paragraph 167, or that the VRS was able to carry out their combat duties once again a function of war without impediment, paragraph 1618, does not meet the test. Indeed the majority conceded during the suspension of salaries, none of the VRS members left the VRS because the VRS military command would not let them. Finally when taking a look at the instrumentality of war, the actual tools that were used to commit the crimes, well, here the record is crystal clear. The Prosecution failed to prove a direct link for any of the crimes committed, the majority specifically acknowledges failure of proof, stating: "The majority recognises that the evidence does not establish that the specific weapons used in committing the charged crimes stem from the logistical assistance process overseen by Perisic." Can't get much clearer than that, and the Prosecution did not challenge this finding. And it's clear from the holding that the aid facilitated by Perisic did not constitute specific direction. Why you may ask? And the answer once again is clear. The majority immediately after recognising this failure of proof rejected that specific direction prong long-held sacred at this institution stating: "However, the majority recalls that the acts of the aider and abettor need not have been 'specifically directed' to assist the crimes." Paragraph 1624. Without this linkage, Perisic cannot be held liable for aiding and abetting. The specific direction test was clearly not met, and the majority certainly erred. There's also another matter that needs to be dealt with which is while a possibility exists that ammunition coming from the VJ was used during the commission of the crimes in Sarajevo, this is certainly not the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence presented. As such, the principle of in dubio pro reo requires reversal since the majority failed to establish that was the only inference to be drawn. And very briefly, if you take a look at the examination of the discussion of the Srebrenica or Selsky bullets, they were specifically found. The only bullets found at Srebrenica were found not to be attributed to the logistical assistance provided by Perisic specifically found beyond a reasonable -- beyond any doubt that it was impossible to attribute those bullets to Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could you give a reference to that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be found in paragraphs 125 -- 1295 to 1302. In conclusion, none of the practical assistance coming from the VJ can be considered to be specifically directed to the commission of crimes so as to support a finding beyond a reasonable doubt that General Perisic aided and abetted those crimes. The majority entirely avoided this analysis in this first instance in finding Perisic guilty. Had the law been properly applied a finding of the actus reus was not proven beyond a reasonable doubt would have been entered counts 1 through 4, the aiding and abetting counts, must be reversed. Clearly if you find the specific direction prong has not been met there's no need to examine substantial effect issue, and I submit to you under the relevant jurisprudence that findings should be made. But you've asked that further question. The unqualified answer is yes to your last question. The Trial Chamber did err in finding the assistance facilitated as substantial effect. The entire analysis concerning substantial effect is predicated upon the majority's unreasonable reliance on dependence and whether it's true or not as somehow being the same as -- when I say by whether it's true or not I'm referring to the dependence, whether or not the dependence is true or not, it's not the same as being a substantial effect of commission of crimes. The question is not whether the VRS substantially depended upon the VJ support to function as an army but rather whether the support of Perisic had a substantial effect on the perpetration of crimes. The dependence of an army as a whole on a foreign army as a whole alone does not automatically lead to the only reasonable conclusion that such assistance provided that dependent army and distributed by that army to its subordinate units, and for an example of that you have the finding in paragraph 1237 that the VRS Koran depot received most of its ammunition from the VJ and it was then distributed out. So the legitimate -- legitimate military delivery of ammunition cannot be attributed to him in terms of what happened to it subsequently because there's no direct link. In Kalimanzira decided a year and a half after Mrksic, this Chamber found that genocidal exhortations in a newspaper prior to the commencement of genocide in Rwanda did not fulfil the actus reus of aiding and abetting even though there was probably a link between the accused's actions and the killings. You found: "There was not enough evidence for a reason trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt that the congruent publications in the first months of 1994 substantially contributed to the commission of acts of genocide between April and July of 1994."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Why wasn't the distribution of arms from the Koran centre not dependent on Mr. Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm saying that the -- that the -- the arms being -- the ammunition being sent to the Koran centre, it does not -- it does not settle the test. Certainly there's a dependency there but that dependency doesn't deal with the link of the crimes because the dependancy there -- if -- if there be such a thing does not deal with the question of substantial effect of the crimes because there are so many different ways that these weapons or ammunition were being used. So you can't draw -- you can't draw a direct link of -- the absence of a direct link you cannot find liability. For -- under the substantial effect analysis. The VRS was entitled to fight and the material provided -- the military logistics was appropriate to that purpose. Crimes committed as a byproduct of bad practices accesses poor command and control deserve punishment admittedly, but declaring the VRS essentially a criminal organisation as a means of affixing criminal liability on Perisic abuses basic concepts of criminal law undermines international humanitarian law and risks casting an inappropriate wide net of liability over state practice that only served to undermine the legitimacy of international criminal law. Lacking direct evidence it is therefore -- this case is therefore based on circumstantial evidence. The law is clear in this regard. Where an inference is drawn from circumstantial evidence to establish a fact upon which a conviction relies it must be the only reasonable inference that could be drawn from the evidence presented. That Perisic contributed to the facilitation of the commission of crimes is not the only reasonable conclusion. An alternative reasonable explanation is the assistance provided by Perisic was direct in supporting the war effort not the commission of crimes and that such assistance did not substantially contribute to those crimes. In addition to the fact that there is no evidence presented intended for those crimes to occur the conclusion of general dependence is insufficient for finding of substantial effect. Suspicion is not evidence speculation based on assumptions is not evidence, and it is certainly not proof beyond a reasonable doubt. General Perisic should be acquitted on counts 1 through 4. I cede the floor to Mr. Bourgon unless you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President. Good morning Honourable Judges of the Appeals Chamber. I have the honour of addressing you this morning in relation to question 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Wait for interpretation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Our answer to this question is straightforward. The Trial Chamber erred in finding that Mr. Perisic had de jure and de facto authority to discipline and to issue command orders to 40th Personnel Centre members. I will address the three prongs of the question. The de jure authority, de factor authority to discipline, de facto authority to issue binding orders. The first topic deals with the de jure authority. The majority's analysis on this issue at paragraphs 1657 to 1667 is circular and does not support the conclusion drawn. The majority's analysis is wrong because it rests on two incorrect premises. First, the majority took the view that the de jure relationship between Mr. Perisic and members of the 40th Personnel Centre was governed by the law on VJ. That is incorrect. I will explain why. Secondly, Mr. Perisic's authority over members of the VJ after they transferred to the 40th Personnel Centre, the majority took the view that there was no change in General Perisic's authority, which is also incorrect. Here is the argument: First of all, the creation of the 40th Personnel Centre was an exceptional situation and something that was not governed by the law on the VJ. From a de jure standpoint, the command and control between the VJ and members of the 40th Personnel Centre was governed on the instructions on Personnel Centres, and that is P734, not by the law on VJ. More importantly, the majority itself confirm at paragraphs 1766 and 1767, that once VJ members transferred to the 40th Personnel Centre, they entered a new chain of command. This altered the de jure command and control relationship. The majority actually stated: "Once a VJ officer complied with an order transferring him to the 40th, he entered the chain of command of the SVK." This actually confirms that the de jure superior from that point on was Celeketic, who was the commander of the SVK. He was the de jure superior. More importantly, VJ members could the not be disciplined by General Perisic once they had been transferred to the 40th Personnel Centre. This is confirmed by Prosecution evidence, and that is P1082. Moving on to de jure authority to punish. The argument is as follows: First of all, the majority relies on its finding of de jure that Perisic was de jure superior and that we have seen is incorrect. Secondly, as found by the majority, Mr. Perisic only used his ability or his purported ability to punish after the fall of the RSK. So the conclusion is simple. There is no proof that at the time of the shelling of Zagreb, Perisic could initiate proceedings against members of the 40th Personnel Centre. Thirdly, the majority in order to infer nonetheless that he could at the time initiate proceedings went to look at evidence of events which took place after the fall of the RSK on 8 August 1995. Now, that's significant, because the fall of the RSK was a major change of circumstances. From that moment on, the SVK and its chain of command no longer existed, so the members of the 40th Personnel Centre were no longer under the command SVK commander, and then it must be recalled that the SVK commander was the de jure superior when Zagreb was shelled. What Perisic could do from both a de jure point of view and a de facto point of view before the fall of the RSK and after the fall of the RSK is entirely different. Consequently, the majority's analysis looking at evidence after 8 August 1995 was flawed from the start. Fourthly, the majority advanced some possible reasons why Mr. Perisic would have waited until after the fall of the RSK to use his powers to initiate proceedings, but that -- the reasons put forward by the majority are flawed. Let me give you just one example. They say Perisic used his authority to punish -- did not use until November of 1995 because he did not need to make use of his authority unless the military objectives of the VJ diverge from those of the SVK. Well, clearly, Mr. President, Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Perisic disagreed whole-heartedly about the shelling of the Zagreb. On 1 May 1995, Mr. Milosevic said to Mr. Perisic in a conversation: "I wish to God that Celeketic would ... can't you tell him not to listen to Martic anymore, please! Martic is going to drag them into a horrible war." How much more can they disagree? Hence, the shelling of the Zagreb would have necessarily triggered the authority of Perisic or the need for Perisic to punish people, to punish members of the 40th. It follows, Mr. President, on the basis of all these arguments that the majority's inference that Perisic could initiate proceedings against members of the 40th at the time Zagreb was shelled is plainly not the only reasonable inference that can be drawn on the basis of the evidence. There's definitely another possible logical and plausible conclusion. He did not do it because he had no authority to do it. Third topic. Authority to issue binding orders. Once again, Mr. President, the majority here rests its analysis on the fact that de jure would have been the -- sorry, that Perisic would have been the de jure superior of members of the 40th Personnel Centre. As I've mentioned earlier, he was not. Celeketic was the de jure superior of members of the 40th Personnel Centre. Secondly, the majority's erroneous finding that Perisic had a general ability to issue binding orders rests on two orders that would have been issued before May 1995, which means before the event or during the event, two orders, both of which do not establish in any way command authority on behalf of Perisic. The first of these orders, 24 March 1995, that's P1925, whether it was obeyed or not - that's one of the Prosecution's argument - is beside the point. This order is clearly not one that establishes command authority over the SVK. The fact that you establish some kind of committee to discuss the assistance given to the SVK does not demonstrate that Mr. Perisic had command authority or could issue binding orders. As for the second of these orders, that's P1800, issued on 7 December 1994. Now, as was highlighted by Judge Moloto in his dissenting opinion, this order can easily be distinguished from an order given within a chain of command. It was sent directly from Milosevic. Celeketic responded directly to Milosevic. Martic was not a member of the 40th Personnel Centre, and Perisic was only instrumental -- instrumental in passing this order along. Once again, Mr. President, this order fails to demonstrate any kind of command authority on the part of Mr. Perisic over the SVK before or when Zagreb was shelled. Now, once again the majority attempted to justify the fact that there was no orders issued until much later, and one of the -- one of the reasons they advance is the fact that Mr. Perisic did not need to use his authority unless the objectives diverge with those of the SVK. I've addressed this argument already. Perisic and Mr. Milosevic both clearly disagreed with the shelling of Zagreb. Had Mr. Perisic had the authority to issue a command order to Celeketic, he would have. He didn't do so because he did not have this authority. Now, on this point, Mr. President, I refer the Appeals Chamber to two cases before the Appeals Chamber, that of General Hadzihasanovic and that of General Blaskic. Blaskic 29 July 2004; Hadzihasanovic 22 April 2008. In both cases, the Appeals Chamber found both of these generals did not exercise effectively control even though they had issued some orders to the alleged subordinate: On the one hand the Mujahedin, that was Hadzihasanovic; on the other hand, the 4 Military Police Platoon that was General Blaskic. Here you have General Perisic did not even issue any order. Now, that's significant. Now, also I refer to Witness MP-80. He stated that Mr. Perisic did not assign task, did not take decisions along classical military lines. That's paragraph 1719 in the judgement, and also transcript 8851. Witness MP-80 also confirmed that Martic was a superior to Celeketic and that Perisic did not issue command orders to Celeketic. The evidence about the relationship between Celeketic and Perisic plainly illustrates that there was neither any de jure or de facto authority on behalf of Perisic to issue command orders. The evidence of MP-80 is critical in this regard because it establishes clearly that neither Perisic or Celeketic believed or acted as though they were in a superior-subordinate relationship. Let me conclude by addressing quickly the system of command and control which the majority stated was bifurcated in two chains of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You have five minutes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll finish in two minutes, Mr. President. From a military standpoint this simply makes no sense. Celeketic followed Martic's order to shell Zagreb and refused to follow Mr. Perisic's attempt to convince him to stop. This makes it clear that Perisic did not have de facto authority to issue orders to Celeketic. Martic's, whose orders were followed, is the one who exercised effective control. If Mr. Perisic would have had de facto authority, he would have simply bypassed Celeketic and ordered directly the Orkan crew, who were members of the 40th Personnel Centre, and tell them to stop. He didn't do that because he did not have the authority to do so. Lastly, Mr. President, I will conclude in saying that in light of all these observation, it is evident that there was no authority on behalf of Perisic to issue binding orders which answers your question and the three prongs of your question. There was no authority on behalf of Mr. Perisic either de jure or de facto to issue binding orders or to initiate disciplinary proceedings at the time Zagreb was shelled. Accordingly, the majority's finding must be reversed. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Do any of my distinguish colleagues wish to ask any questions? I see not. Therefore, we will -- oh, Mr. Lukic, you -- you still have four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I see that I don't have enough effective control over the members of my team but I will try to be as brief as possible and say a few words about the sentence. I am in a very delicate situation. I am supposed to speak about the punishment where once I profoundly believe that General Perisic is innocent. Therefore I held that after your conclusion with respect to the previous appeals -- grounds of appeal, you will not be faced with the consideration of the grounds of appeal 14 to 17. However, on this occasion, I have to point out certain errors committed by the majority that invalidate the sentence of 27 years of imprisonment. By attaching importance to non-relevant facts and by estimating crucial and important facts without providing any statement or reasons for their conclusions and by applying double counting and by reasoning that does not follow the practice of the case law of this Tribunal, the majority committed such errors that make the decision on the sentences completely unsustainable. Our ground of appeal number 14 indicates that there are errors that the majority committed when concluding on the gravity of the crimes and the role of General Perisic. The jurisprudence is ... I will skip this portion and at this point I will address only the submissions contained in our last ground of appeal, ground 17, relating to mitigating circumstances, and I will reaffirm everything that we stated in the appeal's brief under grounds 14, 15, and 16. For interpreters, it is paragraph 20 of the written submissions I gave them. I would like to move on to our last ground of appeal, ground 17, and indicate the errors that the majority committed with respect to mitigating circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We are not getting translation. Could you repeat your sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bearing in mind particularly the mandate of this Tribunal and Chapter VII of the UN charter, acts directed at promoting peace in the territory of the former Yugoslavia were generally accepted as a mitigating circumstance. These are the words of the Appeals Chamber decision in the Babic case, paragraph 71. Peace is always an imperative of the international community. Acts and consequences directed and contributing to peace must be valued especially by the international community. The importance of acts themselves are what you, Your Honours, emphasised in the appeals judgement in Blagojevic, paragraph 330. What matters are acts for promoting peace regardless of the damage that the accused effected. However, the activities and consequences in General Perisic's case, the majority suppressed both with regard to his important activities in achieving peace in Bosnia, that the Trial Chamber found in paragraphs 1365 to 1369, as in the crucial moves that led to the liberation of the French pilots, paragraph 1378 to 1384. The majority in minimalising and even completely rejecting these circumstances uses similar argumentation. They do not consider it to be mitigating circumstances because Perisic in these activities was motivated by military and political interests of the FRY and acted insincerely. By reasoning in this way the majority committed an error. Specific acts and consequences of these acts do not matter to the majority. However, the consequences of the Perisic's -- of Perisic's acts may not be ignored bearing in mind the said values that the practice of this Tribunal respects. I remind you that the Chamber in its judgement quoted evidence that the French President Chirac conditioned the signing of the Dayton Peace Accords on the liberation of the pilots and that Perisic played a crucial role in their liberation, paragraph 1383. Is it possible that anything can override the findings on the acts and consequences of the acts of Mr. Perisic that were directly focused and led to the conclusion of peace in Bosnia. For you, too, Your Honours, the effect and consequences are important. I will remind you in the Appeals Chamber of Dragomir Milosevic in the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Dragomir Milosevic case in paragraph 317 you accepted as a mitigating circumstance the participation of the accused in the agreement on the cessation of sniping. This related to a very important agreement, and although its effect was vastly inferior to that of the Dayton Accords, you concluded at the time that this action by General Milosevic did have a certain positive effect. Through this decision you have shown that the international community does not disregard actions and consequences. The majority in this case did not find it significant and thus committed a discernible error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think your point is clear and we will look closer at it, I can assure you. But we will adhere to the timetable. We will now rise for a pause and resume at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Now we will have the Prosecution, one hour. We will have Prosecution, one hour. My colleagues tell me that the French translation was sometimes came late because of the too great of speed of the delivery of the argument by the counsel for the Defence, and I would ask counsel not to speak too fast to make sure that the French interpreters are not exposed to too much pressure and stress. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We have divided the response to Perisic's appeal in the following way: I will address Your Honours on Perisic's liability for aiding and abetting and will in this context address Your Honours' questions 1 through 4. After that, Ms. Martin Salgado will address Your Honour on Perisic's liability under Article 7(3), and will answer Your Honours' question number 5. And at the end of our submission, Ms. Brady will address Your Honours on sentencing. Before answering Your Honours' questions 1 through 4, we would like to provide some context and shortly address the Prosecution's response in relation to Perisic's liability for aiding and abetting. These are grounds 1 through 12. The focus will be on ground 1, the overarching ground in relation to Perisic's liability for aiding and abetting. Perisic was not convicted for aiding and abetting because he supported the VRS in its war effort. Perisic was convicted because he knowingly gave crucial support to an army whose units systematically committed crimes. He knew that he was giving support that would have a substantial effect on the commission of the crimes of the VRS in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. As Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, Perisic oversaw a system that provided extensive and comprehensive logistical and personnel assistance to the VRS. The units that committed the crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the SRK, and the Drina Corps were among the VRS units receiving that assistance. These units depended on Perisic's support to function as an army and to conduct the operations in Sarajevo and Srebrenica in which crimes were systematically committed. Given that Perisic's support was crucial to units's whose war efforts included the systematic commission of crimes, this support also had a substantial effect on the crimes themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Tell me, please, could Mr. Perisic as Chief of Staff have stopped the aid being sent by his country?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That aid began before he became Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: We acknowledge, Your Honours, that the aid was already in progress when he became Chief of Staff, but he institutionalised the aid and he did nothing to stop it or to channel the aid into legitimate or unlawful purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But could he have done it, you think, in terms of his powers and authority? Could he have said to Belgrade, No more aid, for example?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: If I could have a moment to consult, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the judgement does not -- does not deal with it. All we know is that his persuasive authority in the supreme Defence, called the SDC went the other way. He persuaded them to give him authority to provide assistance. He could therefore also have tried to have used persuasive authority the other way, but because there are no findings in the judgement, we cannot speculate. All we know is he did not make the attempt to do that. Rather, he knowingly gave support to the SRK and the Drina Corps whose units would probably commit crimes as he knew. From the early stages of the war, Perisic was aware of the VRS's discriminatory intent and criminal conduct in fighting the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In relation to Sarajevo specifically, Perisic knew that the SRK was carrying out an unlawful campaign of shelling and sniping, and he knew that they would probably commit more crimes as the siege continued. In relation to Srebrenica, he knew of the grave threat to the enclave. He knew that tensions had already escalated. He also knew of the high probability that crimes would be committed against the population as a consequence of the attack on the enclave, and through numerous sources Perisic became aware that the Drina Corps was, in fact, committing crimes in Srebrenica. He also knew that his acts would assist the commission of these crimes because of the nature and the scope of his assistance and the systematic nature of the commission of the crimes. This is why he was found liable for aiding and abetting, for knowingly providing crucial support to an army whose units systematically committed crimes. Contrary to what the Defence suggests, this does not mean, if one holds Perisic liable for aiding and abetting, that one criminalises any assistance to war efforts. The legal standard does not place unrealistic constraints on waging war or assisting war. Rather, the test for aiding and abetting contains sufficient safeguards against criminalising every form of assistance to an army. First of all, the actus reus requires not any kind of assistance but one which has a substantial effect on the commission of the crimes. Second, the actus reus needs to be coupled with the mens rea, and this requires that the accused has to be aware not only of a small or remote risk that crimes will be committed, but has to be aware of the probability that crimes will be committed. And it is not enough that the accused knows that any crime will be committed. Rather, he needs to be aware of the type of crime that will be committed, which requires awareness of the essential elements, including the mental state of the physical perpetrators. The accused further needs to know that his acts will assist the commission of the crime. And again, knowledge of a small or remote risk is not sufficient. He needs to be aware of the probability that his acts will assist. And this mens rea needs to be present at the time the accused provides assistance. In light of these requirements, the test is far from a strict liability test as the Defence suggests. By providing crucial support to units that systematically commit crimes in the knowledge that they will probably commit more crimes and knowing due to the nature of the support that it would have a substantial effect on these crimes, Perisic meets all of these requirements. Perisic was correctly found liable for aiding and abetting. All grounds in relation to his liability for aiding and abetting should be dismissed. Turning now to Your Honours' question. In the first question Your Honours asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to clarify one question which would help me understand the difficult problems that we have better. Imagine that the Appeals Chamber would feel that aid must be specifically directed in order to enter a conviction for aiding and abetting. Could you point, please, to evidence on the record that would support a conviction for aiding and abetting if we consider this a requirement of specific direction to be a necessary one.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- this depends very much on what is understood by specific direction in order to know what evidence would be required, and with Your Honours' permission, I'd like to address Your Honour's question one first in order to explain what we understand by it. Thank you. In the first question Your Honours asked how should the Appeals Chamber address the issue of specific direction in the context of aiding and abetting liability. Our answer is as follows: The Appeals Chamber in Mrksic, in paragraph 159, has settled the issue by finding that specific direction is not an essential ingredient of the actus reus of aiding and abetting, and there are no cogent reasons to depart from this finding. In ICTY case law, specific direction has, if at all, only ever been discussed as part of the actus reus of aiding and abetting. This actus reus consists of assistance, encouragement or moral support, which has a substantial effect on the commission of a specific crime of the principle. Specific direction is not an essential element of the actus reus, because it is encompassed by its other elements. And I would try to explain our position by going in the following steps: First, I would like to look at the origins of the words "specific direction" in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Second, I would like to look at the interpretation of "specific direction" by the Appeals Chamber in Blagojevic on which the Appeals Chamber in Mrksic relies. And, third, I would like to look at the situation of an accused who is geographically remote from the scene of the crime. Starting with the words, the origins of the words "specifically directed." Your Honours will recall that the notion of specific direction was introduced into the jurisprudence by the Appeals Chamber in Tadic in the context of distinguishing between aiding and abetting liability and liability for joint criminal enterprise. And Your Honours will find on your screen now the relevant paragraph of the Tadic appeals judgement. That's paragraph 229(iii). Can Your Honours see? Do you have it on your screens? Yes? So the Appeals Chamber in Tadic said, and I quote from the beginning of that paragraph: "The aider and abettor carries out acts specifically directed to assist, encourage or lend moral support to the perpetration of a certain specific crime ... and this support has a substantial effect on the perpetration of the crime." So what is required for aiding and abetting are acts which are specifically directed to a certain type of conduct: The assistance, encouragement or moral support, which in turn go to a specific crime. And the Appeals Chamber contrasted that with what is required for joint criminal enterprise and I quote the rest of that paragraph: "By contrast, in the case of acting in pursuance of a common purpose or design, it is sufficient for the participant to perform acts that are in some way -- that in some way are directed to the furthering of the common plan or purpose." So what is required for joint criminal enterprise is any kind of conduct can even be the perpetration of the crime itself, which is directed to the furthering not of a specific crime but more broadly to the common purpose. So this is the context in which that language was introduced. As an objective element, we are discussing here the actus reus, conduct which is specifically directed to assist a specific crime objectively can only mean that it was conduct which was sufficiently connected with the specific crime to provide assistance. It does not make sense in our view to require that the only objective meaning of the act must be to assist the crime, because almost every act could be used for criminal or noncriminal action. This is consistent with the case law of the Furundzija trial judgement, paragraph 243, which said that the conduct of the aider and abettor itself may be perfectly lawful. It only becomes criminal when connected or combined as the Furundzija trial judgement said with the principal's unlawful conduct. And whether the aider and abettor's acts are sufficiently connected to assist depends on the context. Finding that practical assistance provided had a substantial effect on the commission of the crime in question will encompass that it was assistance sufficiently connected with the crime. And this is what the Appeals Chamber in Blagojevic meant when it stated that specific direction will often be implicit in the finding that the accused provided practical assistance to the principal perpetrator which had a substantial effect. That is Blagojevic appeals judgement paragraph 189. And it is important to keep in mind when looking at that Blagojevic appeals judgement that the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 193 concluded its discussion on specific direction by saying that the principal question for aiding and abetting for the actus reus is whether the accused had a substantial effect on the perpetration of the crime. This means that the Appeals Chamber in Mrksic correctly interpreted Blagojevic as meaning that specific direction is not an essential ingredient of the actus reus of aiding and abetting. If we look now at the situation of an accused who is geographically removed from the scene of the crime, the answer in our view remains the same. There is no reason why the legal test should be different in case of geographically removed accused. The Defence does not provide support for their proposition other than pointing to Judge Moloto's dissenting opinion to the trial judgement which itself does not provide further support. Remoteness in our view can be a factor in the Trial Chamber's assessment of the principal question whether on the facts the acts of the accused have a substantial effect on the commission of the crime. So the accused's remoteness may in practice mean that it can be more difficult to show that the conduct had a substantial effect if the accused is far away from the scene of the crime, but this does not change the legal test. And we have also addressed in our response brief in paragraphs 96 to 99 that for aiding and abetting the assistance must not be direct. So the fact that assistance was provided to a depot which then provide it to the units does not mean that the connection is not sufficient. To conclude, as part of the actus reus specific direction is encompassed by the requirement that the aider and abettor must carry out acts of assistance, encouragement and moral support which have a substantial effect on the crime. And just for completeness, we would like to add it is not possible to interpret specific direction as a subjective requirement of aiming at a purpose. And I would just like to remind Your Honours the Defence referred to the language of aiming at in some of the ICTR appeals judgements and we looked at where the language of aiming at came from and it seems to have come from a translation error we might say, because the first time it appeared was, as far as we could find, was in the Ntagerura appeals judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You might be going a tiny bit too fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. The first time it appeared, as we could find, was in the Ntagerura appeals judgement. In the English translation of that Ntagerura appeals judgement, the judgement was rendered in French and in the French in paragraph 370, the Appeals Chamber used the French terms "act qui vise specifiquement a," which is the -- the -- the French phrase that was used from the very beginning when they translated what the Appeals Chamber had said in Tadic. So the French translation did not -- the French original did not introduce new terminology. It was in the English translation of it that the words "aiming at" were introduced, and they were then late reused in other judgements. So aiming at from our point of view simply occurred as a translation error. So it's not possible to understand specific direction as a subjective requirement. The Appeals Chamber in Mrksic in paragraph 159, that is the same paragraph I already referred to, made it very clear the notion of direction forms part of the actus reus, not of the mens rea of aiding and abetting. And more importantly, the mens rea for aiding and abetting is knowledge, and I refer Your Honours generally to ground 7 of our response. And this knowledge standard is incompatible with understanding specifically directed as purpose. This knowledge standard is based on customary international law. It has been applied in this Tribunal and the ICTR for more than 10 years, and it is also applied by other international courts and tribunals such as the Special Court for Sierra Leone, the Special Tribunal for Lebanon, the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia. And there is no cogent reason to depart from this standard of knowledge. Article 25(3)(c) the aiding and abetting paragraph of the ICC statute does not constitute cogent reasons because it was not intended to nor does it constitute an expression of customary international law. The Appeals Chamber in Mrksic in the same paragraph 159 has correctly and explicitly rejected any elevated mens rea standard. To conclude our answer on question 1, specific direction is encompassed in the other elements of aiding and abetting liability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So you are suggesting that the Rome Statute language that the person must have acted for the purpose of facilitating the commission of a crime as a requirement for aiding and abetting is not something that we should take into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. That is not -- it does not constitute a reflection of customary international law. If one looks at the negotiation history, it was a compromise that was negotiated because it couldn't be agreed upon whether the language of intention or knowledge should be used and this is the language that was introduced, but there is nothing to suggest in the -- in the -- in the -- when one looks at how it was established that suggests that the State parties were trying to establish customary international law. Turning to Your Honours' second question: Can aid that is not specifically directed towards a particular crime have the substantial effect required to enter a conviction for aiding and abetting? In a way I've already answered this question in my response to question 1. Only if one were to understand specific direction as a subjective requirement, which it is not, can we even ask the question whether aid which is not specifically directed towards a particular crime can have the substantial effect on the commission of the crime, because then it would be an independent inquiry from the objective requirement of substantial effect, and then the answer would be yes, because it is an independent subjective inquiry from the objective requirement of substantial effect. But as we have explained, specific direction cannot be interpreted as such a subjective requirement. Rather, as I've just explained, specific direction as part of the actus reus is encompassed in the requirement that assistance has to have a substantial effect. If Your Honours follow this position, then the question does not really arise. However, if we were to answer if, the answer would be like this: An act which is not directed as assisting the specific crime in the sense that it is not sufficiently connected to consist in assistance cannot have the substantial effect which is required for aiding and abetting. This means the answer would be no. Turning to Your Honours' third question. Did the aid facilitated by Perisic meet the requirements of specific direction, if any, in the context of aiding and abetting? And I'd like to come back to Your Honour Meron's question at the very beginning asking me to point to specify evidence, because now as I've explained our position, I'm able to refer to that. Only if one were to -- to understand specific direction in the sense of aiming at a purpose, the subjective requirement, would one say that the aid facilitated by Perisic may not have met the specific direction requirement, because the Prosecution's case at trial was never -- and therefore we cannot point to any evidence that it was Perisic who aimed at assisting the specific crimes. But I emphasise again, in our view specific direction means the acts are sufficiently connected with the specific crime to provide assistance and because here the acts were connected with the specific crimes in the sense that his conduct had a substantial effect on them, the answer is yes. And I will elaborate on the substantial effect of Perisic's assistance. So the evidence we would refer Your Honour to is the one we have mentioned in our response brief with regard to grounds 5 and 6, the grounds dealing with the substantial effect. Turning to Your Honours' fourth question then: Did the Trial Chamber err in finding that the assistance facilitated by Perisic have a substantial effect on the commission of the VRS's crimes? The short answer is no. The Trial Chamber did not err. Given the crucial nature of the support that Perisic provided to the VRS units which systematically committed crimes, the only reasonable conclusion is that Perisic's conduct did have a substantial effect on the commission of the VRS's crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. The Trial Chamber found that the logistical assistance Perisic provided and the personnel assistance both as individually as well as accumulatively had a substantial effect on the VRS's crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. And this conclusion is the only reasonable one, because the VRS units in Srebrenica and Sarajevo, the Drina Corps and the SRK, depended on the VJ to fight war. Perisic's support was crucial for fighting that war. That war encompassed the systematic commission of crimes by the VRS. It was not a mere byproduct as the Defence said today. This means that the support provided by Perisic was crucial also for the commission of the crimes and therefore had a substantial effect on these crimes. Perisic was the architect of the system which supported the VRS through personnel assistance and logistical assistance which both had a substantial effect. And I will first address the personnel assistance. Perisic sustained the lifeline of the VRS officers in Sarajevo and Srebrenica by creating and maintaining the personnel centres. Through the personnel centres he ensured that the VJ officers who were serving in the VRS continued to receive their salaries from the VJ and enjoyed all the VJ benefits. Because they were members of the personnel centres, the officers could implement the war strategy which encompassed the systematic commission of crimes in the way they did, without worrying about the basic needs of themselves and the needs of their families. This had a substantial the effect on the crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica, because the key officers responsible for those crimes such as Ratko Mladic, Dragomir Milosevic, Stanislav Galic, Radislav Krstic, Vujadin Popovic, Milan Gvero, Zdravko Tolimir and others were members of the 30th Personnel Centres. They could fight the war which included the systematic commission of crimes without the concerns for their basic needs and those of their families, because the personnel centre system ensured that they received their salaries, their pensions, housing benefits, health insurance and medical assistance. So to conclude, the personnel assistance did have a substantial effect on the crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. In addition to the personnel assistance Perisic also provided logistical assistance which had a substantial effect on the commission of the crimes. Perisic and I referred to that already in the beginning in my answer to Judge Meron's question, he persuaded the Supreme Defence Council to give him legal authority to provide such assistance and he encouraged the SDC to maintain that assistance throughout. He agreed with Mladic on the appropriate procedure by which Perisic would approve the requests for assistance by the VRS. As Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, Perisic therefore oversaw a system that provided comprehensive and extensive logistical and technical assistance the VRS. This included large quantities of ammunition and other weaponry, technical expertise, repair services, fuel, and personnel training. This system under Perisic made it possible for the VRS to function as an army and to fight the war, and among those receiving the assistance were the units we are concerned with, the SRK and the Drina Corps. Because the VJ under Perisic was the key contributor of such assistance, mostly free of charge, the assistance had a substantial effect on the commission of the crimes. Without the system overseen by Perisic, the Drina Corps and the SRK could not have fought the war in Sarajevo and Srebrenica in the way they did, and they could also not have committed the crimes as they did. The Chamber carefully analysed the evidence and provided a detailed factual review. In the following I will focus on the assistance provided in the connection with weaponry. The General Staff of the VJ under Perisic's supervision provided large quantities of weaponry and related assistance to the VRS including to the SRK and the Drina Corps, and this support was provided through three main channels. First of all, weaponry was provided directly to the VRS units including the Drina Corps and the SRK upon request of the Main Staff, and I refer Your Honours specifically to trial judgement paragraph 1062 and 1064. Second, the Koran depot that was the VRS storage depot for weaponry which supplied the Drina Corps and the SRK obtained approximately 70 per cent of its ammunition from the VJ. And third, the VJ General Staff under Perisic provided important logistical assistance to Pretis. Pretis was the industrial company and factory that produced weaponry for the VRS. And this Pretis factory supplied, among others, the Drina Corps and the SRK. Pretis produced large calibre artillery ammunition, shells, mines, and modified air bombs. The VJ General Staff under Perisic was actively involved in practice. It provided support for the production of air bombs. This support included devising the model by which the air bombs were modified, sending experts to solve operational problems with the air bombs and providing the VRS with parts for the air bombs. The VJ General Staff also tested practice weaponry at VJ facilities, and, very important, the VJ General Staff repaired VRS weaponry and overhauled Pretis artillery casing at Kragujevac, a technical overhaul company. Due to this overhaul, the casings could be reused up to five times. In addition to the logistical assistance I have just discussed, the VJ under Perisic's authority also provided fuel, training, and technical expertise to the VRS.
