These different ways of logistical support were so important to the VRS including the Drina Corps and the SRK that it depended on them to fight the war regardless of its other sources of supply. And Mladic and Perisic themselves acknowledged this dependence. Perisic, for example, told the SDC in February 1994 the RS and the RSK certainly can't be defended without our assistance and weapons and military assistance. That's trial judgement 965, Exhibit P782. And Mladic says we would not be able to live without the FRY assistance. That's trial judgement 1598, Exhibit P1282. The Trial Chamber carefully analysed the other sources of supply on more than 20 pages. It found that the logistical assistance that the VRS received from the VJ with Perisic's approval was very important in comparison with other sources. So regardless of the other sources of supply, the VRS, including the Drina Corps and the SRK, depended on the VJ to wage a war, a war that encompassed the systematic commission of crimes. It is therefore inevitable that the Drina Corps and the SRK also depended on the VJ to commit the crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. The Trial Chamber reached the only reasonable conclusion when finding that the logistical assistance provided by Perisic had a substantial effect on the commission of the crimes. Contrary to the Defence's suggestion, this is not undermined by the fact that the Trial Chamber was not able to find beyond a reasonable doubt on the evidence presented in this case that Perisic was involved in providing specific shells and bullets recovered from crime scenes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. And I would like to point out that these bullets were, in any event, only a sample. First of all, there were numerous other forms of practical assistance that I've just discussed. In addition, in light of the amount of ammunition provided, the length of time during which they were provided, no way of channeling them between lawful and unlawful use and the number of crimes committed, it simply would not have been reasonable to conclude that the ammunition provided by the VJ was only used for lawful purposes. Rather, given how crucial the provision of weaponry was for the VRS, their war effort, including the criminal aspect of it in Sarajevo and Srebrenica, would have been much more difficult or even impossible if the VJ had not provided large quantities of weaponry. And this is regardless of whether the Trial Chamber was able to find on the basis of the evidence presented that these specific bullets were provided by the VJ. To conclude, the Trial Chamber reached the only reasonable conclusion: The personnel assistance as well as the logistical assistance Perisic provided had a substantial effect on the commission of the crime by the VRS in Sarajevo and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Counsel, this question, it may sound a bit hypothetical and it will be, but it would help us understand the problems presented by this case, but before asking it, let me repeat something which should be entirely obvious to everybody who knows the practice of this appeals court. When we ask questions, it does not at all mean that this -- they represent our own view. We are probing, because we want to know more about the problems, and this is the spirit in which you should understand my question. Now, assume that the military aid supplied by country B -- A is 100 per cent, is full. So we don't have to worry about the origin of the munition. Assume that it is the entire -- it comprises the entire supply. The country supplies therefore the entire military aid to a warring party in the neighbouring country B. In the neighbouring country B there is a war going on and the recipient engages both in lawful military activities but also in large-scale shelling of civilian towns. Would without more the Chief of Staff of country A be criminally liable?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: The answer to -- to the question depends on whether all the requirements of aiding and abetting are met. So the first question would be is there a substantial effect by the aid on the commission of the crime? So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That's only ammunition and weapons that they have. Assume that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: The question is then how much did the Chief of Staff know when providing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Assume it is known but nothing more than known.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- the question is if, according to our position, if the Chief of Staff is aware of both, that the -- that there is not only a small or remote risk that crimes will be committed, but there is the awareness of a probability of crimes, and he is aware that the assistance provided will probably be used for the -- for the commission of these crimes, then from our point of view the requirements of aiding and abetting are fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. If you want to develop it further. I did not mean to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to add maybe one requirement which comes back to what Your Honour said in the very beginning. The question might also be whether there are ways in this hypothetical scenario to channel the assistance into the use for legitimate purposes and the use for non-legitimate purposes. So this may be a factual question, an additional factual question that Your Honours may have to take into account in deciding on the actus reus and the mens rea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: This would end my submission on the four questions. Unless Your Honours have further questions I would hand over to my colleague, Elena Martin Salgado. MS. MARTIN SALGADO: Good morning, Your Honours. I will be responding to the Defence appeal on superior responsibility and to Your Honours' fifth question. In answer to this question, this is no error. The Chamber correctly found that Perisic had de jure and de facto authority to issue command orders and to discipline the members of the 40th Personnel Centre serving in the SVK. In reaching this conclusion, the Chamber carefully evaluated the evidence and looked at it in its proper context. This was a context characterised by a policy of keeping VJ's links to the SVK secret, and by the pursuit of the overlapping goals of the VJ and the SVK. Under the cover of formal assignment to the 40th Personnel Centre, VJ troops served in the SVK. The 40th Personnel Centre which Perisic created was designed to conceal the links of the VJ to the SVK, not to sever them. It was designed to let the VJ and the SVK pursue their common goals safe from public scrutiny. What the Chamber did was to remove this veil of deception and show Perisic's position of authority and effective control over members of the 40th Personnel Centre. It found that the 40th Personnel Centre members responsible for shelling Zagreb were Perisic's subordinates. This was the right conclusion and Perisic's conviction must stand. Beginning with Perisic's de jure authority, the Chamber unanimously found that Perisic was de jure superior to 40th Personnel Centre members, and I refer you to the trial judgement at paragraphs 1665 and 1668. De jure members of the VJ -- sorry, members of the 40th Personnel Centre were VJ members even while they were serving in the SVK. Perisic was the highest military commander in the VJ, and this means that during the entire period relevant to the indictment, Perisic had de jure authority over the 40th Personnel Centre, which was part of the General Staff. De jure, therefore, his powers over the 40th Personnel Centre members were the same as his powers over the rest of the VJ. He could order and he could discipline them in the same way. That's his de jure authority. Turning to Perisic's de facto abilities to order and discipline members of the 40th Personnel Centre. The Chamber considered these capacities in context and together with other evidence of effective together. I have already spoken about the context of secrecy and the community of goals. Regarding other evidence, the Chamber correctly used Perisic's de jure authority as evidence going to effective control. The Chamber also considered other powers that Perisic had. Perisic could verify promotions and terminate the service of the members of the 40th Personnel Centre who held all the key positions, key commanding positions, in the SVK. Perisic oversaw their salary and other assistance on which the SVK depended. Perisic also received regular reports from the SVK, which allowed him to issue orders to the 40th Personnel Centre members where necessary. Perisic this these powers throughout, and they all support effective control. These powers also corroborate Perisic's ability to order and discipline members of the 40th Personnel Centre. So for example, the Chamber found that terminating military service was a means of disciplining members of the 40th Personnel Centre. Denying promotion where he disapproved of behaviour was another way for Perisic to impose discipline. Before addressing the specific evidence of de facto ordering and disciplining, I would like to emphasise that we are interested in ability, that's ability to prevent or to punish, ability to order or to discipline. While the actual exercise, so the actual issuing of command orders, is relevant to determining ability, it should not be confused with it. As the Trial Chamber found in Popovic, it is ability that evidences superior-subordinate relationship, because to require otherwise would significantly narrow superior responsibilities. Turning to Perisic's ability to issue command orders. Perisic issued command orders before, during, and after the shelling of Zagreb. Again, Your Honours, the number of command orders in evidence needs to be seen in light of the context. Perisic's direct intervention risked exposing the VJ's links to the SVK, something he and the FRY leadership were at pains to keep secret. The number of command orders in evidence is also consistent with Perisic's position at the top of the VJ hierarchy and also needs to be seen in the context of the overlapping goals of the VJ and the SVK. For as long as these goals coincided Perisic did not need to get involved. And against this backdrop, the command orders in evidence significantly demonstrate Perisic's order to issue them. Before the shelling of Zagreb, we have evidence that Perisic issued two command orders. Exhibit P1800 is a command order issued by Perisic on the authority or instructions of Milosevic, who at the time was the President of Serbia. Now, this makes sense because the order was addressed not just to Celeketic, who was part of the 40th Personnel Centre and who was the SVK Main Staff commander, but it was also addressed to Martic, who was the president of the RSK. The order shows that Perisic was considered to have authority over the SVK, and this is corroborated by intercept evidence where both Milosevic and Mikulic, who was the RSK prime minister, expect SVK to follow Perisic. And you can find this evidence cited at paragraph 1727 and footnote 4724 of the trial judgement. Returning to P1800, it was complied with and the compliance report was addressed to Milosevic through Perisic as required by the express terms of the order. The other command order in evidence issued before 2 May 1995 is Exhibit P1925. It was addressed to at least one member of the 40th Personnel Centre, and it is clear from its mandatory terms that it was a command order and this order was followed, and we refer you to the evidence we have cited in paragraph 264 of our response brief. During the shelling of Zagreb on 2 May 1995, Perisic ordered Celeketic to stop the shelling. This also shows that Perisic had the ability to issue command orders. Celeketic, however, followed Martic's order and continued to shell Zagreb the next day. Celeketic did eventually comply with Perisic's order demonstrating that he regarded it as binding and for this we have on 3rd May, 1995, Perisic reporting to Milosevic, "Yes, actions stopped. First I forced him to stop and he stopped." In this regard, the Defence argument that parallel chains of command exclude effective control is contradicted by the case law that we have cited in paragraph 269 of our response brief, but its claim that it makes no military sense to have parallel chains of command is contradicted by evidence that was heard by the Chamber from expert witness General Melvin, and that's at transcript page 9416, 9444, and 2772. After the shelling of Zagreb, Croatia took control over the territory of Western Slavonia. The Defence claims that goals diverged as a result of the Zagreb shelling or during the Zagreb shelling but this is contradicted by evidence that after the shelling Perisic continued approving requests for assistance. And you can find some of that evidence cited at paragraph 1246 of the trial judgement. What happened after the shelling of Zagreb was that Perisic decided to become more involved in controlling the SVK, and this shows that he had the ability all along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Just to remind you, counsel, you have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARTIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Celeketic was replaced as commander of the SVK staff and he was replaced at Perisic's behest by another member of the 40th Personnel Centre, Mile Mrksic. The evidence that Mile Mirkovic did not take orders from President Martic but instead from Perisic confirms Perisic's ability to issue command orders. Before and during Operation Storm in August 1995, Perisic issued several command orders to members of the 40th serving as SVK corps commanders. Mandatory language of the orders confirms they are command orders. In particular, during Operation Storm, Perisic ordered to address and if necessary execute "all scaremongers." This shows him intervening at corps level to maintain discipline in the SVK as the SVK approaches defeat. The order also demonstrates Perisic's power to discipline to which I turn. Perisic could and did initiate disciplinary and/or criminal proceedings against members of the 40th. He did so when the SVK surrendered and the RSK fell in the hands of the Croatian forces. Importantly, investigations focused on the conduct of the 40th Personnel Centre while they had been serving in the SVK, and by seeking to discipline these officers for their dereliction of military duty while serving in the SVK, Perisic showed his connection to them. And this is the reason proceedings were never formally pursued as they risked exposing the VJ's intervention in the war in Croatia. Instead as punishment, service was terminated. The Defence argues that Perisic only took these disciplinary measures after the fall of the RSK when in their argument new command and control relationships came about. But they do not substantiate this argument with any evidence. In fact, during this entire time, there was no systemic change in Perisic's powers over the members of the 40th Personnel Centre. He did not acquire more powers after the shelling of Zagreb or after the fall of the RSK. Throughout, he was Chief of the General Staff. The other indicators of the effective control continued the same. His authorities and effective control continued the same and it included his power to issue command orders and to discipline. Perisic does not show an error in the finding that he chose not to exercise these powers rather than he could not do so. The Chamber saw through the facade the 40th Personnel Centre and analysed the reality of Perisic's relationship to its members, and for this reason his appeal on superior responsibility should be dismissed. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This brings to an end -- Ms. Brady.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I clearly have even effective control over my team than Mr. Lukic has over him because I obviously have only two minutes left. Your Honours, I was going to make a few comments about Mr. Perisic's sentence in light of the time we can largely rely on our briefs, safe to say that the 27-year sentence that was imposed upon Mr. Perisic is not manifestly excessive. Its entirely appropriate given that Mr. Perisic's crucial role in assisting and facilitating these crimes which were of the greatest magnitude. Today Mr. Lukic has focused on the mitigating factor especially in relation to Perisic's apparent efforts to promote peace. In our submission the Chamber was properly placed to determine how genuine those efforts were and what weight to accord them, and in fact in our submission the Chamber within the bounds of its discretion were correct in giving no weight to his advocating for peace during the war and in that respect also the French in relation to the release of the French humanitarian workers and UNPROFOR hostages because of their finding that he did not genuinely work towards peace, having found in essence that his actions were motivated by political expedience rather than altruism. And the same goes in relation to the release of the French pilots. Your Honours, in summary, to conclude Prosecution's response to the Defence's appeal, a 27-year sentence is appropriate. He hasn't either today or in his brief shown any discernible error that would warrant a reduction. The sentence reflects the gravity of the underlying crimes themselves in Srebrenica in Sarajevo and in Zagreb, and his 7(3) responsibility for Zagreb and his contribution to those crimes. We ask that you dismiss all grounds of the appeal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady. We will now have a 20-minute pause and resume at 11.50 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Reply by Mr. Perisic's counsel, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have resumed the control over my team, so I'm going to address you first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm terribly sorry. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly I'm going to say something about the sentence, because obviously this part received the least attention today, and I'm relying on the submission made by the Prosecution. Today, they claim that the Defence of Mr. Perisic in its appeals brief failed to point to any significant error committed by the majority on the basis of which the sentence could be reduced. I'm not going to repeat all the errors that we pointed out in our brief, but very briefly, I can only say now that the Defence has clearly demonstrated that the majority has committed an error in assessing the gravity of the crime, because in its judgement, it weighed it with regard to the objective gravity of crimes and not in light of the specific crimes of which it found General Perisic guilty. Specifically, in relation to the Srebrenica crime, the only arguments contained in the judgement pertain exclusively to the crime of extermination of which Mr. Perisic was acquitted. As for the crimes in Sarajevo the majority relies on the crime of terror for which Mr. Perisic was not even charged and it relied on the four-year period of the siege of Sarajevo which is beyond the indictment period, since we know that he was chief of the VJ General Staff for a much shorter period. Another thing that I would like to underline is an error that appears in two grounds of the appeal in a similar way, both with respect to individual acts committed by the accused, or his role in the crimes that should be established by the Trial Chamber whilst weighing the gravity of crimes, and with respect to the facts that the Chamber took as aggravating circumstances concerning the abuse of authority. In both cases, the majority did not provide any argumentation but solely entered a finding of the fact. I would remind you of your standard from the judgement in -- where you say that the Trial Chamber should provide conclusions with the written statement of reasons in order for the person found guilty be able to -- to counter it and for the Appeals Chamber to be able to understand the reasoning of the Trial Chamber. Nowhere in the judgement there is any finding that they found that the actions of Mr. Perisic were unlawful. Nowhere in the judgement, likewise in the conclusions relating to the gravity of the crimes and regard to the role of Mr. Perisic, there is nothing more than the sentence which says that he held the position of the VJ Chief of General Staff during the relevant period. Therefore, both you and the Defence are at a loss to conclude what was taken into account and what was not taken into account. Now, as for mitigating circumstances, what I said today is in a way related to what was written in our brief, and that is that you, by relying on your practice, I mentioned the Milosevic case, you are the ones who are going to evaluate the actions and the consequences, and this is what has to be taken into account with regard to mitigating circumstances. In that sense, motivation cannot carry more weight than the mitigating circumstances such as, for example, a contribution to peace. In the Milosevic case, as I said, you made a judgement that his contribution to putting a stop to sniping campaign was so significant that it was described as a mitigating circumstance. And I may -- must make another analogy, and it concerns mitigating circumstances in our grounds for the appeal 17. This concerns the findings in the conclusion the relating to the saving of 700 ABH soldiers who -- who swam over the Drina in 1995. The majority committed an error by saying that that was not a mitigating circumstance, because Perisic himself by providing assistance to the VRS had contributed to the circumstances that they found themselves in. I would like to remind you as the Appeals Chamber, in the Krajisnik case you took into account as a mitigating circumstance that he helped some of the non-Serbs who were in detention despite the fact that he was one of the persons who created conditions for those people to be detained. In Dragomir Milosevic case, you, the Appeals Chamber, following the findings of the Trial Chamber, you found him guilty of having commit -- in order for the crimes to be committed, and then on the other hand his participation in peace negotiations you took into account as a mitigating circumstance. In that sense, I think that this is a major error that the majority disregarded the fact that Perisic contributed to the saving of more than 700 members of the ABH through his intervention with Mr. Milosevic, and this should have been evaluated as a significant mitigating circumstance. Now I'm going to give the floor to my colleague Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. President. I will address question 5 and the arguments raised by the Prosecution in this respect. Let me begin very quickly, Mr. President, by addressing the argument that was not touched on by the Prosecution when they spoke about Celeketic. I said in my address to you this morning that Perisic, when Celeketic refused to follow his advice to stop the shelling because he disagreed, if he had had the authority over members of the 40th Personnel Centre, he could have gone to the Orkan crew and say, Stop it. That's what a commander does when a commander has control over an entity composed almost entirely where all the key officers are from the 40th Personnel Centre. The majority did not look at this issue at all. The majority failed to note that Perisic did not do that. And that is very important, Mr. President. Why is it so important? Well simply because Perisic did not do that for two reasons: One, he respected the chain of command of the SVK; and, two, he knew that he did not have the authority to bypass Celeketic. That's the key indicator of effective control. Now, when Milosevic spoke to Perisic, he never suggested to Celeketic, Hey, Momo, go straight to the 40 -- to the Orkan crew and tell them to stop. He never said that. Milosevic also understood that there was no such thing as authority of Perisic over the 40th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: A few quick words on de jure. The Prosecution referred to this this morning and I would like to come back because they referred to what I call is the circular argument, the circular argument which I referred to which is what the majority did. The majority said the perpetrators are members of the 40th Personnel Centre. Check. Good. The 40th Personnel Centre members are part of -- are the VJ. I'll give that to them. Check. That's good. Mr. Perisic is the highest military officer in the VJ. I'll give it to them. Check. But the question is: So what? How does that establish any type of de jure relationship? What the Prosecution failed to do and what the majority also committed -- where the majority committed the error is by failing to take into account that once the members of the VJ were transferred to the 40th Personnel Centre, they moved into the SVK chain of command. If you move into the SVK chain of command, where is Perisic in the SVK chain of command? He's not there. In the SVK chain of command you have Martic, Celeketic, Orkan crew and all these other people, nobody else. Perisic is not in that chain of command. And the Prosecution did not -- neither address the instructions, that's P734 or P1082. Now, I say Prosecution, but I could also say majority, because the majority did not take this evidence into account in deciding that there was a de jure relationship. I move on, Mr. President, to the fact that at page 55, lines 6 to 9, the Prosecution said this morning that there was something, that the actual exercise of authority was relevant but that what really mattered is ability. Well, they're right. I'll give -- that's a correct argument. But the problem is the actual exercise is of the highest relevance, and here you have no evidence that there were command orders issued by Perisic before or during the shelling of Zagreb and that Perisic did not initiate any -- any disciplinary proceedings before or during the shelling of Zagreb. Now, if you don't have this, you have to supplement this with something else in order to come with a finding that the only reasonable conclusion is that Perisic could do those things, but there is no -- that evidence is not there. There's a couple of assumptions. One of these assumptions is the fact that the goals diverge, and because he did not need to do so. Well, that's a nice theory but it's not proof. The Prosecution said this morning in its address the difficulty is it's not because Perisic -- Perisic continued to give support even though after the shelling of Zagreb continued. Again, I say so what? I'm told to conclude, Mr. President, so I will conclude immediately. I'm not going to come back on the orders issued by -- by Perisic. That's 1800 or 1925. They do not establish any type of command. What the Trial Chamber -- what the Appeals Chamber must look for is to evaluate in the context the type of relationship that Perisic had with the SVK. Did he exercise command over the SVK which comprised mainly of 40th Personnel Centre officer? That's why I referred the Appeals Chamber to Blaskic and to Hadzihasanovic. Again, the Prosecution argument fails to address this issue, because when you compare the two, you can come to only one conclusion, Mr. President, and that is that the majority erred in finding that there was something called a superior to subordinate relationship between Perisic and Celeketic. And lastly I'll conclude simply by saying that the element or criteria advanced by Judge Moloto which we took in our brief and we took in our reply again was not addressed. When two people believe or act -- unless they believe and they act as though they are in such a relationship, they are not in such a relationship, Mr. President. If I say I have to force someone to do something, I'm certainly not into an effective control relationship. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith will pick up from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The response to the question: Could he stop the aid being sent through his country? The answer is -- is very clear. The answer is no. It's an unqualified no and the Prosecution should have answered the question [indiscernible]. And the reason is very simple. He's not the president of the country. He was not the SDC. He was not involved in the Ministry of Defence. And what you -- your question deals with an entire state and the way that a state behaves. He is one component part of the state, but he is not the state which is why it is so important to take a look at and recognise the importance of personal culpability. I want to ask -- I want to ask a question where -- where do we think we're going right now? Where do we think the law right now is going? Because in terms of the hypothetical that you put forth, Your Honour, the answer is really very clear. We see case after case after case around the world right now where you have what you call rebel movements, self-determination movements that fall precisely into your fact pattern where crimes are being committed as we see them being committed. So each and every nation state that gives assistance to those rebels or to the other side is guilty of aiding and abetting. Now, do we think there's going to be prosecutions throughout the world for the United States and its personnel or for the United Kingdom or for France or for NATO? I think not. And the problem that's going to occur and it's going to occur very, very rapidly will be that there will be a rise of impunity, because there will be a recognition that there was not equal treatment under the law, because certain states or certain people we prosecuted and others will not. The more powerful will not. And if there's any doubt about what the view is, what's being pedalled right now, I suggest to you that we listen to the following and the following comes from a conference on the 20th of August, 2012.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Moderator: For students to take. So the next question is what was the most important legal precedent set by your Tribunal this year and explain why and what you think the precedent means for the greater development of international criminal law. We'll begin again with Serge. "Serge Brammertz: Thank you. I would like to say a few words about the Perisic judgement from September last year. Perisic, he was the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav army, and as such providing logistical support to the Serbian Army in Bosnia. So he was prosecuted for aiding and abetting crimes committed in -- on the territory of Bosnia, crimes for which many people have been convicted already in the past by the Tribunal. The Trial Chamber has considered him and found him guilty for aiding and abetting those crimes, a number of crimes, murder, inhumane acts, persecution, attacks on civilians, aiding and abetting. Those crimes committed as said by the army in Bosnia. He was, however, acquitted for aiding and abetting the crime of extermination in Srebrenica because the Trial Chamber was of the opinion that the mens rea was not there at that level, that he was fully aware there was a policy of committing crimes but not to the level of extermination or genocide. He was also convicted for -- as a superior for having failed to punish those responsible for crimes committed by the shelling of Sarajevo. It was an important judgement. Twenty-seven years was the sentence. Why is it important? Because it is partially precedent, I think so, which shows that providing assistance to a party in the conflict, by knowing that this party is implementing a policy in which crimes are committed, that this person can be prosecuted for aiding and abetting crimes, and we speak here about logistical support in the sense of paying salaries out of Belgrade, providing fuel for -- for tanks, by providing training, and we're even not speaking about weapon in this -- in this case because the Trial Chamber was of the opinion that the evidence was -- was clear that also weapon had been provided by the Chief of Staff of people under a specific responsibility, but that there was no factual link established during the trial between the weapons which had been delivered and the crimes committed in a number of municipalities. So I think it is an important development in this sense that aiding and abetting is receiving, I think, a larger interpretation. Of course, we have to wait for -- for an appeals decision but I think it's a quite interesting development."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Following along with what Mr. Brammertz the Prosecutor said and going back to your hypothetical, Your Honour, we'll have the following situation: None of the weapons whatsoever are supplied by country A. They supply everything else. Same fact pattern. Country A is guilty of aiding and abetting. Without a doubt. Salaries, fuel. Now, the fact of the matter is here, because the case is, and I return to this, a circumstantial case against Mr. Perisic, obviously the only reasonable inference to be drawn is -- is what's necessary for purposes of the finding of guilt. And I said that badly, and I think you know exactly what I meant. There can only be one inference, and it can be only the reasonable inference, and here there are alternable reasonable inferences, and I'll cite you to the record because in the record it is very clear with regard to the issue of fuel which Mr. Brammertz talks about at paragraphs 168, 169, 170, there's clear indication that the VRS was getting fuel from other places. With regard to the issue of salaries was discussed beforehand. VRS members, the core VRS members, stayed when they weren't being paid. They didn't leave. They continued to remain active without the benefit of those salaries. So if you don't have salaries and you don't have fuel as -- as being attributed to General Perisic, what you really are left with is what I said at the -- at the end of my first presentation, which is you have speculation. You may not like the way it feels, you may think that maybe something should be different, but that's not what we do in a court of law. In a court of law is we prove beyond a reasonable doubt by facts not by speculation. And the Prosecution in effect in their argument has conceded that the case against General Perisic was not proved. I despise war. I do not believe there is an individual in this courtroom that likes it, but the fact of the matter is wars are waged and horrible things occur. And increasingly with the way the world is developing, we have knowledge of those horrible things occurring. Now, if this court wishes to make the determination that war should cease, and I'm not talking about the crime of aggression, but that war should be criminalised, then do so. Then do so. But please, remember, that when he was a general, when he was supporting his country, when he was concerned about doing his job, that was not the law. General Perisic should be acquitted of all counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. I take it the Defence has completed its presentation, and I would ask Mr. Perisic whether he would like to use his ten minutes to make a personal statement. I see the answer has already been provided. So, Mr. Perisic, you have ten minutes. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes, I do wish to do so. Your Honours, thanks to you, this is my last opportunity to address you. I was pondering what could I say to you out of the scope of the Defence case presented that would enable you to additionally assess me as a person and as a general who performed certain duties. When this trial started on the 3rd of October, 2008, I addressed the Trial Chamber, and inter alia I said and I quote: "I deeply regret the victims of crimes committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and I sincerely sympathise with their families. Any loss of life is an irreparable loss for society and a life taken through crime is the worst of all losses. I believe that all those who committed crimes will be prosecuted and appropriately punished. I wish that war crimes will never be repeated again. As a professional officer, I hate war, because I'm aware that any war, particularly the ethnic, religious, and civil war that took place in the territory of Yugoslavia was something that was the worst thing that could happen to all the peoples of the region." This is my deep conviction, and that's why I wanted to repeat it. I believe that in this case you are facing numerous challenges not only with respect to my responsibility but also to the fairness of the sentence pronounced, the sentence of 27 years' of imprisonment and the impact that it has on the credibility of this court. I'm not a lawyer. I never had a desire or the need to engage in law, but nevertheless, I can conclude that the judgement and the verdict does not reflect what I heard in the course of this trial. During the 40 years in military, I could not but develop deep respect for the law and its significance. The experience that I gained in the military makes it even more difficult for me to understand the judgement. I cannot understand the decision made by the majority of the Trial Chamber, and therefore I'm asking how can something be established beyond a reasonable doubt if the Presiding Judge has doubts? By sheer logic, something like that is untenable, because it is impossible. I am a Serb by ethnicity. I am a professional soldier who served throughout Yugoslavia during his career. I was the chief of the VJ General Staff during a long period that encompassed some troubled years of the conflict. I had been told that due to my nationality and the position that I held, it would be nearly impossible to expect that my trial was going to be objective, unbiased, free of prejudices, and views taken in advance. Despite of that, immediately upon the receipt of the indictment, I publicly declared my trust in this court, which was carried by the media and which was admitted into evidence as part of the Defence case. I came to the Tribunal voluntarily two days before the indictment was published, which is a unique case of the respect for the Tribunal. In spite of everything negative that has been happening to me to this will date I sincerely hope that you are above this and that you are going to judge me objectively and impartially. My case is unique in the world. Never before was a chief of the General Staff of an army indicted and convicted for crimes that were committed by members of another army in another country. You are the Judges who are going to render a decision in accordance with your conscience and your sense for justice, but you have to do some soul searching if the decision that you make should have far reaching consequences to any Chief of General Staff of any army including NATO and other alliances as well as the policies pursued by other countries that are assisting wars currently being prosecuted in Afghanistan, Libya, Syria, Sudan, Yemen and elsewhere where crimes were committed and are still being committed. My direct superior, the president of the FRY and the President of the Supreme Defence Council, Zoran Lilic, who issued orders to me to provide assistance to the VRA and the SVK was neither indicted nor convicted. General Celeketic, for whom the Court has established that he was responsible for the crimes resulting from the shelling of Zagreb was neither indicted nor convicted. Instead, I am convicted for his crimes. You know very well that the decision to provide assistance to the VRS and SVK was taken as a political and state decision long before I was assigned to the position of the Chief of General Staff of the VJ. As chief of the General Staff I participated in the decision taken by the SDC and the government of the FRY which pertained to the assistance in waging a war not for the commission of crimes as concluded by the majority. Your Honours, I defended my state and its citizens professionally and honourably from being pulled into the war. I proposed and implemented certain measures in a timely and responsible manner pursuant to the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council for the purpose of preventing the spill-out of war from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina to the territory of the FRY. Before taking over as Chief of General Staff, the FRY and the SFRY before it were in war -- were at war with Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And after I was replaced by Chief of the General Staff the FRY waged war with NATO and the Kosovo Liberation Army. I'm proud that the FRY and its army while I was Chief of the General Staff did not participate in war for more than 50 years. Every officer, especially a general, has the duty to envisage and foresee the developments in the environment and their consequences on the security of its area of responsibility and to propose and take preventive measures for its protection. In my case, that area of responsibility was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There is nothing pleasant about war for a normal person. Very often there is no choice, and even if there is some, every activity leads to grave consequences. This is well known to all armies, to all state policies, and despite everything, however hard and distasteful it sounds, the world did not prohibit the waging of war or rendering assistance to others at war. Essentially everyone in this courtroom, everyone who follows these proceedings and millions of others are fully aware that assistance to the waging of war is given every day depending on the interests and policies of various states. For example, France and the US were involved in armed conflicts and extended support to forces in conflict thousands of kilometres away from their territories in order to protect their own interests. They did not have to suffer any consequences for it. This is quite different from the situation I was in, because assistance to Republika Srpska and its army and the Republic of Serbian Krajina and its army was extended in order to protect the territory of our own state, of my own state, the FRY, from the conflict that were taking place at its footstep. What would you have expected me to do as Chief of General Staff of the VJ? What did the majority of the Trial Chamber which convicted me expected me to do as Chief of General Staff of the VJ when there was a war raging around us and threatening to spill over into the FRY? As a professional soldier heading a military structure that implemented the decisions of the SDC and the FRY government, my actions during my entire military service, including the period for which I was indicted, were aimed at preventing the expansion of war and based on domestic and international law. I express my deep regret for all the victims of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. I feel for the pain and suffering of all the citizens of the states where there is a war going on. I would be happiest if all wars stopped in the world this moment, but it seems that despite my wishes, this is not going to happen. If the majority of the Trial Chamber believed that with my conviction all wars would stop, they should have said so, but they noted instead that although war results in devastation and suffering, it is not a crime, but it still convicted me very dramatically for it. Your Honours, while Judge Moloto, the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber, analysing the situation in which I was believed that I should go home, two other Judges decided that I should be in prison for 27 years. Something like this is hard not only to understand but to live with. Does it not contain in itself the confirmation of the existence of a reasonable doubt? I believe that you, Your Honours, will repair this injustice. Thank you for allowing me to address you and your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perisic for your personal statement. Before we conclude, I would like to thank the parties for their arguments today and for their significant preparatory work over the course of this appeal. I with like to thank my colleagues on the Bench, but we are most extremely grateful for the hard work and dedication of the interpreters and translators, the court reporters, the staff of court management support services, and the information technology support teams. The high quality of their work allows us to proceed with our cases fairly and expeditiously, and this would not be possible without their commitment. The hearing is now concluded, and the judgement of the Appeals Chamber will be delivered in due course.
